concepts.name: Confidentiality
concepts.originator: The Hippocratic Oath (Hippocratic school of Kos; author unknown)
concepts.place: Island of Kos (Cos), Aegean Sea, Greece
concepts.definition: Whatever I see or hear in the lives of my patients, whether in connection with my professional practice or not, which ought not to be spoken of outside, I will keep secret, as considering all such things to be private.
concepts.plainSummary: The oldest idea in the file: privacy as a promise made by the person who is let in — the healer swears to keep to himself what he sees and hears in a patient's life.

sources.institution: U.S. National Library of Medicine, History of Medicine Division
sources.title: Greek Medicine: The Hippocratic Oath (translation)
sources.quote: Whatever I see or hear in the lives of my patients, whether in connection with my professional practice or not, which ought not to be spoken of outside, I will keep secret, as considering all such things to be private.
sources.note: English translation published by NLM with its 2008 display on Greek medicine (curated by Michael North). The Greek text is conventionally dated to the late 5th or 4th century BCE; the date is approximate.

sources.institution: U.S. National Library of Medicine, History of Medicine Division
sources.title: Greek Medicine: Hippocrates
sources.quote: Virtually nothing is known of the first physician named Hippocrates, but there are considered to have been several, all of them teachers at the famous medical school on the Mediterranean island of Cos. It was in the 5th century BCE, however, that Hippocrates’ name and image began to emerge as a leader in medical research and thought.

concepts.locationNote: Coordinates of Kos town; the Oath is associated with the Hippocratic medical school on Kos, but its authorship and exact date are unknown.

concepts.name: The home as castle
concepts.originator: Sir Edward Coke, reporting Semayne's Case (Court of King's Bench)
concepts.place: Court of King's Bench, Westminster Hall, London
concepts.definition: That the house of every one is to him as his Castle and Fortress as well for defence against injury and violence, as for his repose
concepts.plainSummary: Privacy as walls: the law limits when even the King's sheriff may break into a house, and a householder may shut the door on an officer who does not follow procedure.

sources.institution: Online Library of Liberty (Liberty Fund), from The Selected Writings of Sir Edward Coke, vol. I
sources.title: Sir Edward Coke declares that your house is your “Castle and Fortress” (1604)
sources.quote: That the house of every one is to him as his Castle and Fortress as well for defence against injury and violence, as for his repose
sources.note: Semayne's Case, 5 Co. Rep. 91a, 77 Eng. Rep. 194 (King's Bench, Michaelmas term 1604); transcription from Coke's Reports as edited by Steve Sheppard for Liberty Fund.

sources.institution: Online Library of Liberty (Liberty Fund)
sources.title: Sir Edward Coke declares that your house is your “Castle and Fortress” (1604)
sources.quote: If the Sheriffs did not follow the correct procedure in issuing writs, then the home owner had the right “to shut the door of his own house” in their faces.
sources.note: Editorial gloss by the Online Library of Liberty on Coke's report.

concepts.locationNote: King's Bench sat in Westminster Hall; Coke published the report in part 5 of his Reports (1605).

concepts.name: The right to be let alone
concepts.originator: Thomas M. Cooley (phrase, 1879); Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis (Harvard Law Review, 1890)
concepts.place: Harvard Law Review, Gannett House, Cambridge, Massachusetts
concepts.definition: the right to life has come to mean the right to enjoy life--the right to be let alone
concepts.plainSummary: Faced with the snapshot camera and the gossip press, two Boston lawyers argue that the common law already protects a person's 'inviolate personality' against publication — borrowing Judge Cooley's phrase 'to be let alone'.

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review, vol. 4, no. 5 (reproduced by the Louis D. Brandeis School of Law Library, University of Louisville)
sources.title: Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis, 'The Right to Privacy'
sources.quote: the right to life has come to mean the right to enjoy life--the right to be let alone, the right to liberty secures the exercise of extensive civil privileges
sources.note: Originally published at 4 Harv. L. Rev. 193 (dated 15 December 1890).

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review, vol. 4, no. 5 (reproduced by the Louis D. Brandeis School of Law Library, University of Louisville)
sources.title: Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis, 'The Right to Privacy'
sources.quote: Recent inventions and business methods call attention to the next step which must be taken for the protection of the person, and for securing to the individual what Judge Cooley calls the right "to be let alone."
sources.note: Originally published at 4 Harv. L. Rev. 193 (15 December 1890). Footnote 10 cites 'Cooley on Torts, 2d ed., p. 29'.

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review, vol. 4, no. 5 (reproduced by the Louis D. Brandeis School of Law Library, University of Louisville)
sources.title: Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis, 'The Right to Privacy'
sources.quote: Instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life; and numerous mechanical devices threaten to make good the prediction that "what is whispered in the closet shall be proclaimed from the house-tops."

concepts.locationNote: Publisher's location (the Harvard Law Review, Cambridge, Mass.); Warren and Brandeis practised law together in Boston.

concepts.name: Privacy as control over information
concepts.originator: Alan F. Westin, Privacy and Freedom (Atheneum)
concepts.definition: Privacy is the claim of individuals, groups, or institutions to determine for themselves when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others.
concepts.plainSummary: Westin moves privacy from the house to the data: it is a person's claim to decide who learns what about them, and when — the definition that underpins 'notice and choice' and the Fair Information Practices.

sources.institution: Journal of Social Issues, vol. 59, no. 2 (Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues / Wiley)
sources.title: Stephen T. Margulis, 'On the Status and Contribution of Westin’s and Altman’s Theories of Privacy'
sources.quote: Privacy is the claim of individuals, groups, or institutions to determine for themselves when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others.
sources.note: Margulis reproduces Westin's definition from Privacy and Freedom (New York: Atheneum, 1967), p. 7, as a block quotation (p. 412 of the article). The book itself is in copyright and was not read directly; copy hosted by HSE University, Moscow.

sources.institution: Washington and Lee Law Review, vol. 25 (1968) — book note
sources.title: Privacy and Freedom. By Alan F. Westin. New York: Athenum. 1967.
sources.quote: The book was written under the auspices of the Special Committee on Science and Law of the Association of the Bar of the City of New York, with financial support from the Carnegie Corporation, and will undoubtedly stand as a major reference work on the subject.
sources.note: Contemporary book note confirming the 1967 New York (Atheneum) publication. Read via Internet Archive snapshot because the repository blocks scripted access.

sources.institution: International Association of Privacy Professionals (IAPP)
sources.title: Westin’s Privacy Scholarship, Research Influenced a Generation
sources.quote: Westin is considered by many to have been the first intellectual to espouse a new definition of privacy.

concepts.locationNote: Westin was professor of public law and government at Columbia University; the book was published by Atheneum in New York.

concepts.name: Informational self-determination
concepts.originator: Bundesverfassungsgericht, First Senate (Census Act judgment, BVerfGE 65, 1)
concepts.place: Federal Constitutional Court, Karlsruhe, West Germany
concepts.definition: This fundamental right confers upon the individual the authority to, in principle, decide themselves on the disclosure and use of their personal data.
concepts.plainSummary: Germany's constitutional court strikes down parts of the 1983 census law and declares a fundamental right to decide, in principle, who may learn and use one's personal data.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court of Germany)
sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209, 269, 362, 420, 440, 484/83 (Census Act) — official English translation
sources.quote: This fundamental right confers upon the individual the authority to, in principle, decide themselves on the disclosure and use of their personal data.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court of Germany)
sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209/83 et al. (Census Act) — official English translation
sources.quote: A societal order, and its underlying legal order, would not be compatible with the right to informational self-determination if citizens were no longer able to tell who knows what kind of personal information about them, at what time and on which occasion.

sources.institution: Deutschsprachiges Fallrecht (DFR), University of Bern — text of BVerfGE 65, 1
sources.title: BVerfGE 65, 1 – Volkszählung
sources.quote: Das Grundrecht gewährleistet insoweit die Befugnis des Einzelnen, grundsätzlich selbst über die Preisgabe und Verwendung seiner persönlichen Daten zu bestimmen.
sources.note: German original of headnote 1. Translation: 'To that extent the fundamental right guarantees the power of the individual, in principle, to decide for himself on the disclosure and use of his personal data.'

concepts.name: Decisional privacy
concepts.originator: U.S. Supreme Court, Griswold v. Connecticut (opinion of Justice William O. Douglas)
concepts.place: Supreme Court of the United States, Washington, D.C.
concepts.definition: The present case, then, concerns a relationship lying within the zone of privacy created by several fundamental constitutional guarantees.
concepts.plainSummary: Privacy as freedom to make intimate decisions without the state: the Court strikes down Connecticut's ban on contraceptive use by married couples.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States — United States Reports vol. 381 (Library of Congress digital collection)
sources.title: Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965)
sources.quote: The present case, then, concerns a relationship lying within the zone of privacy created by several fundamental constitutional guarantees.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States — United States Reports vol. 381 (Library of Congress digital collection)
sources.title: Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965)
sources.quote: Would we allow the police to search the sacred precincts of marital bedrooms for telltale signs of the use of contraceptives?
sources.note: Opinion of the Court by Justice William O. Douglas; argued 29-30 March 1965, decided 7 June 1965. OCR text of the official U.S. Reports scan.

concepts.name: Privacy as contextual integrity
concepts.place: Washington Law Review, University of Washington School of Law, Seattle
concepts.definition: Contextual integrity ties adequate protection for privacy to norms of specific contexts, demanding that information gathering and dissemination be appropriate to that context and obey the governing norms of distribution within it.
concepts.plainSummary: Privacy is not secrecy but appropriate flow: information shared in one context (the clinic, the bank, among friends) carries that context's norms, and moving it elsewhere can violate privacy even if it was never secret.

sources.institution: Washington Law Review, vol. 79 (pre-publication manuscript hosted by Stanford University's PORTIA project)
sources.title: Helen Nissenbaum, 'Privacy as Contextual Integrity'
sources.quote: Contextual integrity ties adequate protection for privacy to norms of specific contexts, demanding that information gathering and dissemination be appropriate to that context and obey the governing norms of distribution within it.
sources.note: Manuscript marked 'Forthcoming: Washington Law Review, 2004' (dated 2/6/04); published as 79 Wash. L. Rev. 119 (2004). The published PDF on the UW repository blocks scripted access.

sources.institution: Washington Law Review, vol. 79 (pre-publication manuscript hosted by Stanford University's PORTIA project)
sources.title: Helen Nissenbaum, 'Privacy as Contextual Integrity'
sources.quote: The central thesis of this Article is that the benchmark of privacy is contextual integrity; that in any given situation, a complaint that privacy has been violated is sound in the event that one or the other types of the informational norms has been transgressed.

concepts.locationNote: Publisher's location; Nissenbaum was then at New York University.

concepts.name: A taxonomy of privacy harms
concepts.originator: Daniel J. Solove (University of Pennsylvania Law Review)
concepts.place: University of Pennsylvania Law School, Philadelphia
concepts.definition: In the taxonomy that follows, there are four basic groups of harmful activities: (1) information collection, (2) information processing, (3) information dissemination, and (4) invasion.
concepts.plainSummary: Instead of one definition, Solove maps sixteen kinds of harmful activity — from surveillance and aggregation to exclusion and decisional interference — grouped by where in the data's life they occur.

sources.institution: University of Pennsylvania Law Review, vol. 154, no. 3 (copy hosted by Yale University, Department of Computer Science)
sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'A Taxonomy of Privacy'
sources.quote: In the taxonomy that follows, there are four basic groups of harmful activities: (1) information collection, (2) information processing, (3) information dissemination, and (4) invasion.
sources.note: Published version, 154 U. Pa. L. Rev. 477 (January 2006). The Penn Law repository copy blocks scripted access.

sources.institution: University of Pennsylvania Law Review, vol. 154, no. 3 (copy hosted by Yale University, Department of Computer Science)
sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'A Taxonomy of Privacy'
sources.quote: Privacy is a concept in disarray. Nobody can articulate what it means.

concepts.locationNote: Publisher's location; Solove was then at George Washington University Law School, Washington, D.C.

concepts.name: The person as first party (VRM → MyTerms)
concepts.originator: Doc Searls and ProjectVRM (Berkman Klein Center, Harvard); later the IEEE P7012 working group
concepts.place: Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts
concepts.definition: Customers must be able to proffer their own terms of engagement —and to have auditable records of all contracts to which both sides agree.
concepts.plainSummary: Flips the direction of the contract: instead of accepting a company's terms, the individual (through a software agent) proffers standard privacy terms that the company agrees to — the idea standardised as IEEE 7012 'MyTerms'.

sources.institution: ProjectVRM, Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society, Harvard University
sources.title: ProjectVRM wiki: Main Page — VRM Principles
sources.quote: Customers must be able to proffer their own terms of engagement —and to have auditable records of all contracts to which both sides agree.

sources.institution: ProjectVRM (projectvrm.org), via Internet Archive snapshot of 28 December 2025
sources.title: Doc Searls, 'The MyTerms PAR'
sources.quote: With MyTerms, the person (and their electronic agent) is the first party, and the corporate entity (with its agent) is the second party.
sources.note: projectvrm.org blocks scripted access; read through the Internet Archive. The post quotes the IEEE P7012 Project Authorization Request.

sources.institution: ProjectVRM, Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society, Harvard University
sources.title: ProjectVRM wiki: About
sources.quote: It is a project of the Berkman Center for Internet and Society at Harvard University, and is led by Doc Searls , an alumnus fellow of the Center (he was a fellow there from 2006-2010).
sources.note: The project began during Searls's 2006-2010 Berkman fellowship; the wiki's Main Page adds that its blog was hosted at Harvard from 2007 to 2023.

concepts.locationNote: ProjectVRM is hosted by the Berkman Klein Center; Searls later worked from the Ostrom Workshop, Indiana University, Bloomington.
